idiom_name: hand-written struct array + column-descriptor table (fed by sqlite3_step / libpq PGresult)
implementation_notes: C has no standard tabular container, so the record set is a hand-written triple: a column descriptor (name plus declared type per column), a contiguous array of row structs, and accessors that resolve a column name once and then read by index. The database APIs supply only the pieces - sqlite3_step() yields SQLITE_ROW per row, after which sqlite3_column_count()/sqlite3_column_name() give the header and the sqlite3_column_*() family reads the current row, while libpq hands over the whole materialised result as PGresult with PQntuples/PQnfields/PQfname/PQgetvalue. What replaces the classic structure is therefore your own struct plus accessors: the library types cannot themselves travel as the value, because PGresult is owned by libpq (PQclear) and sqlite3_column_text() pointers are invalidated by the next step.
pitfalls: SQLite hands out pointers into the statement's row buffer: a cell taken from sqlite3_column_text() dangles after the next sqlite3_step(); copy every value into owned storage while building the set.
A column's declared type is only an affinity in SQLite - sqlite3_column_type() can differ per row - so an int field can silently receive text; carry the actual per-value type or convert explicitly.
Row and column counts are plain size_t with no bounds checking: resolve the column index once through the descriptor and assert it, or the first typo reads the wrong cell.
